Airbnb's AI-Native Transformation: Reading the AI-First Organization Through the CEO's Earnings Statements and the CTO's Testimony
Introduction: One year after saying Airbnb would become an "AI-first application," the company declared it had "rebuilt itself as an AI-native company."
On August 6, 2025, Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky stated during an earnings call,
In the coming years, Airbnb will become an "AI-first application."

Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
One year later, on August 6, 2026, Airbnb declared in its earnings announcement that it had fundamentally rebuilt Airbnb as an "AI-native company."
The conversation has shifted from the app to the nature of the company itself.
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
"So, what is the AI-first organization that Airbnb is aiming for?"
The headline "AI wrote 60% of the code" does not answer this question.
While the 60% figure indicates a change in the volume of work, it does not explain who is doing what within the organization.
I interpret the basis for the AI-first organization Airbnb is aiming for by dividing it into two categories.
The first is the materials Airbnb has released to investors, such as earnings announcements, earnings calls, and filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The second is the content shared by Ahmad Al-Dahle, who became CTO in January 2026, in an interview with AI-specialized media outlet Latent Space (published October 2, 2026).
Airbnb CTO Al-Dahle previously served as the head of generative AI at Meta and led the development of "Llama," the AI model that Meta released for anyone to use.
"Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience"
The earnings materials show the results achieved in numbers, while the CTO's interview describes the target organizational image in words.
Notably, Latent Space has named Airbnb's approach "inside-out AI." This term is used by Latent Space and is not Airbnb's own terminology.
Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience

Figure 1: Airbnb's earnings show the destination in numbers, while the CTO describes the target organizational image in words
Chapter 1: Airbnb handed over coding tasks and primary customer support to AI
First, I will list the milestones that can be confirmed in the earnings materials.
As of the first quarter of 2026, approximately 60% of the code generated by engineers at Airbnb is written in collaboration with AI.
CEO Chesky described this same figure as "written by AI" during the earnings call, adding that Airbnb estimates this to be roughly double the industry average.
The scope of this figure is "code generated by engineers," not the entirety of Airbnb's existing codebase.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
The number of features and improvements released between January and June 2026 increased by approximately 80% compared to the same six-month period the previous year. For major initiatives, the time from conception to delivery was reduced by up to 60%.
For customer support, an AI assistant serves as the first point of contact for inquiries.
The percentage of consultations initiated by the AI assistant that were resolved without human intervention rose from approximately one-third in the October-December 2025 quarter to over 40% in the January-March 2026 quarter. By the April-June quarter, this reached approximately 45%, and the number of supported languages exceeded 50.
The denominator is "consultations initiated by the AI assistant," not all inquiries.
As of August 2025, this AI assistant was built by combining 13 models and fine-tuning them with tens of thousands of conversations.
Figure 2: Airbnb support features an AI assistant that responds first, while maintaining a path to human agents.
The change is also reflected in costs.
Support costs per booking in the April-June quarter fell by approximately 16% year-over-year. During the earnings call, CEO Chesky explained the reason, stating, "Part of it is due to improvements in the AI assistant."
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
In the August 2026 earnings call, CFO Ellie Mertz stated that "the vast majority is due to AI agents."
The AI agents referred to here are the support AI assistants.
There is some variation in how management describes the reasons for the same figures.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The quarterly report (10-Q) filed with the SEC is a bit more specific.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, the use of AI in support reduced the number of inquiries handled by human agents, resulting in a $17 million reduction in costs paid to external contractors.
At Airbnb, much of the coding work and the initial response to inquiries have been handed over to AI.
What remains for engineers after coding work shifts to AI is covered in another article, so please refer to it below👇
Chapter 2: Airbnb changed its approach to giving small teams clear missions and releasing features as soon as they are ready.
CEO Chesky has repeatedly explained the methodology behind these numbers during earnings calls.
Give small, elite teams clear missions, release simple improvements to learn, and focus efforts on what works.
In the February 2026 earnings call, Chesky stated that he began this approach two years ago and expanded it company-wide after confirming it worked.
They have also stopped hoarding features for launch events, releasing them as soon as they are ready.
Regarding the performance for the April-June 2026 quarter, CEO Chesky stated that the reason was not a single product or initiative, but a combination of execution, talent, and an AI-accelerated approach.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
CEO Chesky does not view the utilization rate of AI tools as a metric for success.
He called the figure that over 80% of engineers use AI tools a "vanity metric," stating that what matters is the company's culture and its ability to adapt to change.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The role of humans is also beginning to change.
CEO Chesky stated that Airbnb "must move at the speed of AI," indicating that management roles focused solely on overseeing people will not be as necessary as they once were. He also mentioned that design and engineering managers are returning to hands-on coding work.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
CTO Al-Dahle goes even further.
He ended the practice of creating requirements documents and handing them off from designers to engineers, instead having planning, design, and development teams deliberate from the start using working prototypes.
Al-Dahle's belief is that companies organized by purpose and outcome, rather than by function, are stronger in the AI era.
However, regarding the future of team structure, Chesky himself stated that "it is too early to say." Organization by outcome is the CTO's policy and is not the final form of the company known as Airbnb.
What about the number of people? At the end of 2025, there were approximately 8,200 employees.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, personnel expenses in the operations and support departments increased by $27 million due to an increase in average headcount. The number of employees has not decreased.
Marts explains that because the output and speed obtained from current employees have increased significantly, there is no need to increase headcount as much as in the past.
Chapter 3: Airbnb has kept the judgment of complex and sensitive cases in the hands of employees
While there are tasks that Airbnb has handed over to AI, there are also judgments that have been left in human hands.
According to the annual report (10-K) filed with the SEC, as of the end of 2025, Airbnb has entrusted the majority of support inquiries to approximately 13,000 outsourced personnel. Internal support employees focus on complex and sensitive cases.
CEO Chesky called AI-based customer support the "hardest problem for AI." This is because incorrect answers are not permitted, and urgent cases or matters involving trust and safety must be accurately handed over to humans.
CTO Al-Dahle also says that they intentionally choose which cases to have AI solve and decide which cases not to leave to AI yet.
Even in the development field, a line is drawn between AI and humans.
According to CTO Al-Dahle, many teams have begun automating system monitoring and primary response to failures (on-call).
When a monitoring alert is triggered, an agent (a mechanism where AI proceeds with procedures on its own) is activated to determine whether it is a problem. If there is a problem, it issues a pull request (a proposal for code changes; hereafter PR), and an engineer reviews the PR.
If it is a false alarm, the agent closes the case itself.
Figure 3: A diagram of the flow where an agent determines Airbnb's on-call status and a human reviews the PR
The name of the figure above is "Handed over to agents," but CTO Al-Dahle's words are that many teams are "beginning" automation.
In the on-call flow, the initial determination of whether it is a problem is handled by an agent. What remains for humans is the judgment of whether or not to incorporate the PR proposed by the agent as code.
Figure 4: Airbnb separates where AI is entrusted with primary judgment and where humans make judgments
CEO Chesky also stated that regarding AI spending, he judges not by the amount of tokens (units of text processed by AI) used, but by how much product was released and the quality of the design.
It is also humans who decide not to make AI usage volume itself a goal.
Chapter 4: CTO Al-Dahle requires that even for PRs written by AI, the person who created them must explain them
What Airbnb leaves as a human role is not just judgment.
What CTO Al-Dahle strongly demands is that every engineer be able to explain what they created, even if it is a PR created by AI.
Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience
After leading Meta’s Llama models, Ahmad Al-Dahle is now tran
Behind the above is a concern for young engineers.
Experienced engineers have acquired judgment through the experience of shipping systems, running them in production, and failing.
Now that AI handles many tasks, can young people gain the same experience?
Al-Dahle believes that if they continue to be required to explain things, young people can also learn interface design, the structure of the entire system, and the importance of testing.
"Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience"
However, the policy of requiring the creator to explain is something that was mentioned in the CTO's interview.
I could not find any description to the same effect in the three earnings calls and earnings announcements I checked. Whether it is a rule of the company Airbnb or the CTO's policy cannot be distinguished from public documents.
The quality of AI output depends on the experience and judgment of the person using it.

Chapter 5: Airbnb is building up the context gained from previous services into the next ones
In May 2026, Airbnb expanded its services to include grocery delivery and airport transfers. In the August 2026 earnings call, CEO Chesky stated that newer services could be built faster than before, revealing that grocery delivery took 8–9 months to develop, while airport transfers took about 6 weeks.

Airbnb adds AI search, more social features
Airbnb is evolving in two directions: On the ground, it wants to compete with hotels by providing myriad services; online, it is using AI and people in its Airbnb network to aid travel discovery.
As part of its fall product update, the company is adding services to the app it had launched last year, such as meal delivery, laundry, baby-gear rental, ski and boat rental in limited locations, and expanded grocery delivery.
The second big feature is AI search. The company has taken a cautious approach to rolling out AI features, with CEO Brian Chesky opting to stay away from a chatbot-like interface. Earlier this year, he teased the new search feature for property discovery.
Now, users can switch on a toggle to search for properties via text or voice prompts. Once you start the search, the interface will show you dynamic filters based on your preferences. For instance, if you type “baby” in the AI search filter, Airbnb will automatically show you further filters like cribs, playgrounds, or children’s books and toys.
The platform is also using AI to bring out relevant features of a property, and will let you compare properties in your wish list by way of AI-powered summaries and reviews.
“We are finally making our first foray into AI search. And what you see is just the very beginning of something. And over the coming months, we’re going to really be iterating this very quickly. It’s not hard to create AI search; it’s hard to create AI search in e-commerce when you have $100 billion going through your platform,” Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky told TechCrunch.
“Anyone can vibe-code a search function, but to do something that doesn’t kill conversion rate, that’s the hard part.”
The company is also doubling down on social features that nudge people to take more trips and book additional experiences such as food tastings and craft workshops. Last year, the app started allowing users to connect with fellow travelers and friends on its platform.
Now, travelers can look at a map based on their connections’ past or upcoming trips. When you tap on a trip, you can see where your connection stayed, and which experiences they sought out. For those conscious about their privacy, there’s an option to not share their trips with others as well.
Airbnb is also building pages about neighborhoods based on guest reviews and other sources to help travelers discover places to eat and things to do.

Why Is ABNB a Good Business?
Founded by Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia in their San Francisco apartment, Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) is the world's largest online marketplace for lodging, primarily homestays.
1. Nights and Experiences Booked Drive Additional Growth Opportunities
As an online travel company, Airbnb generates revenue growth by increasing both the number of stays (or experiences) booked and the commission charged on those bookings.
Over the last two years, Airbnb's nights and experiences booked, a key performance metric for the company, increased by 9.3% annually to 148 million in the latest quarter. This growth rate is solid for a consumer internet business and indicates people are excited about its offerings.
2. EBITDA Margin Reveals a Well-Run Organization
EBITDA is a good way of judging operating profitability for consumer internet companies because it excludes various one-time or non-cash expenses (depreciation), providing a more standardized view of the business's profit potential.
Airbnb has been a well-oiled machine over the last two years. It demonstrated elite profitability for a consumer internet business, boasting an average EBITDA margin of 35.6%. This result isn't surprising as its high gross margin gives it a favorable starting point.
3. Excellent Free Cash Flow Margin Boosts Reinvestment Potential
If you've followed StockStory for a while, you know we emphasize free cash flow. Why, you ask? We believe that in the end, cash is king, and you can't use accounting profits to pay the bills.
Airbnb has shown terrific cash profitability, driven by its lucrative business model and cost-effective customer acquisition strategy that enable it to stay ahead of the competition through investments in new products rather than sales and marketing. The company's free cash flow margin was among the best in the consumer internet sector, averaging an eye-popping 36.8% over the last two years.

HSBC upgraded Target to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold’ and raised its price target to $190 from $125. A Delaware judge ruled that Liquidia’s Yutrepia infringes two United Therapeutics (UTHR) patent claims. Both offer inhaled treprostinil treatments for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and PH-ILD . United sells Tyvaso products, while Liquidia’s Yutrepia, approved in 2025, is a dry-powder competitor. Next year, Airbnb will mark its 20th anniversary. Through its evolution—from a few air mattresses placed on an apartment floor to one of America’s best-known American technology companies—it has been led by Brian Chesky. And at a time when Silicon Valley doesn’t champion introspection, Chesky, 45, is an outlier: someone who has become a prominent voice on company leadership and a frequent investigator of his own character. “The primary weakness of me as a founder running a company was people had to pay for my immaturity in my thirties,” he told me during a recent interview at Airbnb’s headquarters in San Francisco for our new interview series, The CEO Moment. “But I said it was a good long-term bet,” We spoke as the company, called out by critics as contributing to rising housing costs in the cities where it operates, was set to announce a number of new housing initiatives.
You are one of three people who started the company in 2007. There aren't that many founders leading Fortune 500 companies. How do you think the fact that you founded this company shapes how you lead it today?
The people that build companies tend to be more in the details, more decisive, bigger authority, …They tend to take bigger, bolder risks partly because they have the moral authority to. For example, I could—I wouldn't—but I could change the name of the company because I came up with the name of the company. Somebody who is a professional manager, I don't think they would ever dare change the name of their company. They would feel like it's not theirs to change.
You’ve said that you think CEOs think about hiring wrong. Why is that?
Because I thought about hiring wrong…When I was starting Airbnb…Sam Altman…said hiring should be 50% of your job. I'm not even sure it was 50% of his job.
Has your thinking about the value of remote work shifted as we’ve gotten further from the pandemic?
I have a view that if your office policy's is easy to explain, it might be wrong because it might be one size fits all.
You’re vocal about the fact that you think leaders don’t need to have regular one on one meetings with their direct reports.
I think it's not only unnecessary, it's probably inferior. And if you go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones…
Now you can get a hotel on Airbnb. Why?
I was ideologically against hotels. In fact, I think our first tag line was “forget hotels.” So why would I ever offer them? And so that was my party line for probably 10 years. In 2018, 2019 my stubbornness got the best of me and many of our customers told us that we want hotels. And ultimately I had to make a decision. You know if you're a brand, just because your customer wants something doesn't mean you sell it to them. You can decide no, go somewhere else…But we noticed there were three types of people. There are people that only book Airbnbs. There are people that only book hotels, but most people are willing to book both.
You're building your own AI frontier lab separate from Airbnb. Why not build that within Airbnb and what will be the relationship between the two?
I thought about building inside of Airbnb….I like to think that our shareholders know what they get themselves into, and I never sold them on us being a frontier company and spending billions and billions of dollars of capital expenditure and then spending huge sums recruiting these engineers or these AI researchers….The benefit to Airbnb and to me is I'm gonna learn a lot about AI, but it's also a totally different kind of culture. So I wanted to keep them separate.
You’re announcing a number of new initiatives around housing. People say Airbnb makes cities more expensive. What role do you want the company to play in making places more affordable?
I think Airbnb has been a place people pointed to over the last 15 years, especially the last decade…for reasons why cities are expensive. And so we have wanted to be part of the solution, not part of the problem.
We're creating a $250 million fund to house the last dollar for projects. There's about 750,000 homes in America development projects that are stalled because they don't have the last dollar of completion ... .We want to do something called the City Index. We want to open source data around cities, policies, the cost of living, permitting to basically show the cities that are most successful at lowering housing costs by having the best policies….We want to do the housing prize where we're going to do a million dollar prize every year for five years for any company, private or or nonprofit that has ideas around technology that can make housing development easier.

Booking (BKNG) vs Airbnb (ABNB): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
Booking Earns More on Every Dollar:
The operating gap between them is wider than their reputations suggest. Booking turns 34.41% of revenue into operating profit. Airbnb manages 21.01%.
That thirteen-point gap is the whole difference between the two models. Booking lists rooms somebody else built, insured, and staffed, while Airbnb has to police millions of individual hosts it does not employ.
The cash follows. Booking produced $7.73 billion of levered free cash flow against $3.21 billion at Airbnb. Earnings grew 117.90% at Booking in the most recent quarter, which is not the profile of a business in decline.

Airbnb Grows Faster and Owes Nothing:
Here is what the share prices have been responding to. Airbnb grew revenue 16.50% in the most recent quarter against 8.10% at Booking. For investors paying for growth rather than for margin, that is the number that matters.
The balance sheets are a genuine contrast. Airbnb holds $12.07 billion of cash against $2.50 billion of debt, so its enterprise value of $78.62 billion sits well below its market value of $88.19 billion. Booking is the other way round, with $20.92 billion of debt against $17.21 billion of cash.
Airbnb also earns 34.54% on equity, which is a strong figure and reflects how little capital the business needs. The supply is the difference nobody can copy quickly. Airbnb's inventory is millions of homes that no hotel chain owns, and no competitor can simply build.
Booking is the cheaper of the two and one of the few large travel names trading below the market multiple. You can find more of them here.
The Valuation Case:
Sustainability sits with Booking. Hotel commissions recur because hotels have no better way to fill empty rooms, and the business has survived every attempt to disintermediate it.
Airbnb's growth is faster, but its supply is individual hosts, who are more easily tempted elsewhere than a hotel chain with a distribution contract.
On price, the gap is stark. Booking trades at 13.28 times forward estimates against 25.38 times for Airbnb, so an investor pays roughly half as much for each dollar of next year's profit.
The PEG ratio settles whether that discount is deserved. Booking's is 0.61 and Airbnb's is 1.42, which means the cheaper stock is cheap even after adjusting for its slower growth. We ranked the alternatives here.
Conclusion:
Booking is the better of the two. It earns a wider margin, produces more than twice the free cash flow, trades at little more than half the forward multiple, and has fallen a quarter while its earnings more than doubled last quarter. However, Airbnb is growing twice as fast and carries net cash rather than net debt. It also owns supply that cannot be recreated. An investor choosing Booking is being paid to accept slower growth, which on these multiples looks like the better trade.

Online travel stocks, listen, those names have sold off periodically since the launch of ChatGPT based on the same general idea that the bots can easily replace them. Operational Differentiation and Network Insulation
Airbnb, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:ABNB) operational model relies on a highly fragmented, non-standardized supply base that inherently resists simple aggregation. Unlike traditional online travel agencies that distribute uniform hotel rooms through centralized global distribution systems, the company offers over 9 million active listings managed directly by private hosts. Standardizing or crawling millions of independent property listings, house rules, pricing algorithms, and individual host communications presents a significant hurdle for autonomous AI booking agents.
In addition, the company's direct traffic profile remains among the strongest in the digital consumer space, with nearly 90% of traffic coming direct or organically. The direct consumer relationship insulates the business from rising search engine marketing costs while posting a 35% adjusted EBITDA margin in the second quarter
Valuation, Relative Premium, and Downside Risks
Trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of roughly 25.4x, Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) carries a significant valuation premium over the broader sector median of 14.55x. While the premium highlights the company's superior cash conversion, strong net cash position, and dominant brand mindshare, it also creates a valuation risk if travel demand decelerates. High valuation multiples leave little margin for error if macroeconomic pressures dampen international leisure spending or if regulatory tightening across major metropolitan markets limits inventory growth. If booking growth slows, the stock's elevated multiple could face compression regardless of its competitive insulation against AI competitors.

According to Insider Monkey database metrics tracking 1000+ hedge fund portfolios, 75 hedge funds held positions in Airbnb, Inc. The company showed in recent quarters that its platform can generate strong free cash flow even during slow consumer environments. pages.title: How Airbnb.org And Rotary Are Giving Displaced Australians The Gift Of Shelter
pages.text:
Top Stories:
Ex-NFL reporter Michele Tafoya a GOP candidate
LISMORE, AUSTRALIA - MARCH 31: A father and his young daughter inspect a flooded street on March 31, 2022 in Lismore, Australia. (Photo by Dan Peled/Getty Images)
In 2022, floodwaters tore through Lismore, a town in northern New South Wales, in a once-in-a-century event that washed whole neighborhoods away. Rotary volunteers brought in foldable housing pods, compact homes built inside shipping containers, so families had somewhere to sleep. Four years later, some of those pods still haven't come back.
"At times, the recovery is a very long recovery," says Mahir Momand, CEO of Rotary Australia World Community Service (RAWCS). "It could take years for people to then be able to rebuild their houses, to go back to their houses."
Insurance claims stall. Government schemes move slowly. Families live away from home for months that stretch into years, and the strain lands on their mental health. After the Lismore floods, the community suffered a painful rise in suicides, and RAWCS added mental health support to its work there.
Momand understands displacement from the inside. In Afghanistan, he founded and led Community Banking Network. Then the Taliban attacked him, leaving bullet scars in his shoulder, and he fled to Australia as a refugee. "I was running a large organization," he says. "And then a few weeks later, I was in Australia. I was no one." Doctors diagnosed him with post-traumatic stress disorder.
"There's nothing normal," he says of that upheaval. "The environment is not normal, the people around you are not normal."
That experience shapes how he thinks about recovery. It also helped drive a new partnership that gives displaced Australians something rare in an emergency, the power to choose where they sleep.
Mahir Momand, CEO of Rotary Australia World Community Service (RAWCS)
RAWCS supports 1,008 Rotary clubs and about 23,700 Rotarians across Australia. Its projects reach 45 countries, yet roughly 30% of its 470 active projects sit in Australia alone, and that share has grown over the past decade.
"We in Australia should not be needing this type of support," Momand says. In a wealthy nation, he argues, governments should carry that load. Climate change is pushing in the other direction. "There'll be more natural hazard events in Australia," he says. "And the intensity of these natural hazard events will increase as well."
He describes a recent stretch when Queensland flooded, Victoria burned and South Australia entered its second year of drought. "One country, three neighboring states, three different types of disasters," he says. RAWCS and local Rotary clubs responded in each with housing pods, hay for farmers' livestock, mental health support and even haircuts. They also handed out $500 cards, which give people fast cash when the local bank has burned down.
The scale of the risk is enormous. More than 6.5 million Australian homes face exposure to natural disasters, and around 23,000 people are displaced each year by floods, bushfires and cyclones.
Airbnb.org, the nonprofit founded by Airbnb, approaches the problem from another direction. It provides free temporary housing to people in crisis, and since 2020 it has delivered more than 1.6 million nights worldwide.
"When you think about the world of emergency housing, these homes exist already," says Christine Chang, Director of Global Programs and Operations at Airbnb.org. "We don't have to swing in, we don't have to build anything and then take it down."
Any home listed on Airbnb can host an Airbnb.org guest, and the nonprofit pays the host for each night. That matters in towns where disaster has wiped out tourism and damaged hosts' own properties. What Airbnb.org needs are trusted local partners who know which families need help most.
Australia sits high on its list. "Australia, for all of its natural beauty, is plagued by a lot of natural disaster," Chang says. "And every year, tens of thousands of people are impacted by that."
Airbnb.org knew RAWCS's long record in disaster recovery and reached out. This August, the two announced a national partnership. "A partnership with an organization like Rotary is the way that we're going to be able to reach into all of these communities in Australia," Chang says. She sees Rotary's strength in its unusual shape. "It's a huge organization globally, but the way it shows up in each community is so local," she says. "And so grassroots."
Christine Chang, Director of Global Programs and Operations at Airbnb.org
Momand walks through a hypothetical. A bushfire hits Orange, a town in New South Wales, and the government declares a disaster. Families who lost their homes contact the Rotary Club of Orange, which vets them and passes their details to RAWCS. RAWCS refers them to Airbnb.org, which loads credits onto their Airbnb accounts. Each family can then book a home for 28 days.
"What we're doing here is we're giving people agency," Momand says. A family of six with two dogs needs a different home than a retired couple. With credits in hand, each household picks the size, location and setup that fits.
Momand credits governments with the core response, from evacuation centers to food and clothing. "The government does that heavy lifting there, and government should be given credit for that," he says. "But what we do is we fill the gap, and that gap is to give people that choice to actually stay in a place that works for them."
In an evacuation center, he notes, "everyone would go to the same place, everyone would be treated the same, and sometimes that may not work for people."
A Century-Old Network Meets A Modern Platform
Rotary has been providing community service in Australia for 105 years. Momand describes the partnership as a meeting of that history and modern technology. "We're marrying that community support with the 21st century platform of Airbnb," he says.
Emma Bell stands on both sides of that marriage. She is a Rotarian, and she rents out a four-bedroom farmhouse outside Mudgee, New South Wales, on Airbnb. "As an Airbnb host, I already open my home to people from all walks of life," she says. "This partnership gives me, and hosts across Australia, the opportunity to do that in a way that genuinely helps people through one of the most difficult periods of their lives."
Each organization brought what it already had. RAWCS brought trust, built over a century, club by club. Airbnb.org brought millions of homes and software that matches people to them in seconds. Together they deliver help faster, and on families' own terms.
River Ranch Mudgee, the farmhouse Rotarian Emma Bell lists on Airbnb in Central West New South Wales
Momand believes this is "probably the first time that a organization like Airbnb.org and a not-for-profit like us are partnering at a national level of this magnitude." Rotarians in New Zealand have already asked to bring the model home. "They already love the idea," he says.
So far, Airbnb.org has supported eight disaster responses in Australia, providing close to 1,800 nights of free accommodation. With a Rotary club in nearly every town, that number has room to climb fast. Chang's long-term goal is for every one of Airbnb's nine million-plus homes to host an Airbnb.org guest at least once.
For the next family forced out by flood or fire, help could arrive as a booking confirmation and the key to a home they picked themselves.

Airbnb (ABNB): Is ABNB’s Strong Growth Story Already Priced Into the Stock?
On August 7, 2026, Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) reported Q2 2026 results.
Revenue grew 17% year-over-year to $3.6 billion, ahead of analysts' $3.57 billion estimate, while gross booking value rose 16% to $27.2 billion. Net income totaled $816 million and adjusted EBITDA reached $1.3 billion, a 35% margin, up over 100 basis points year-over-year. The company's free cash flow was $1.3 billion for the quarter and $4.8 billion over the trailing twelve months. Management raised full-year revenue growth guidance to at least mid-teens and lifted the adjusted EBITDA margin outlook to at least 35.5%.
But Airbnb's latest Wall Street debate didn't start with September's target hikes. Here's why one analyst was already warning that the stock's strong fundamentals had become part of the problem.
Booking (BKNG) vs Airbnb (ABNB): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
Hotels, AI Efficiency, and Record First-Time Booker Growth are Winning Over Wall Street
Citizens analyst Matthew Condon raised his target on Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) to $200 from $190 on September 18, keeping Outperform and naming Hotels and AI-powered pricing as key catalysts through 2027. Raymond James upgraded ABNB to Outperform from Market Perform on September 8, lifting its target to $200 after a deep dive reinforcing confidence in durable low double-digit growth. Rosenblatt's Scott Devitt initiated coverage on September 1 with a Buy rating and a $220 target, the highest of the four, arguing focus is shifting toward new businesses starting to show results.
The quarter supported that view.
Nights and seats booked grew 10%, an acceleration from Q1, and app bookings rose 23%, now 64% of total nights booked. First-time bookers grew 11%, the fastest pace in four years, led by Gen Z, while expansion markets grew roughly twice as fast as core markets. Management credited an AI overhaul of search, checkout, and pricing for cutting support costs per booking by 16%. Hotels remain a single-digit share of nights booked but are growing about three times faster than core rentals, and CEO Brian Chesky said host interest has recently surged.
One Analyst Thinks the Good News is Already Priced In, and the Stock's Own Reaction Agrees
Morgan Stanley assumed coverage on September 16 with an Equal Weight rating and a $170 target, the lowest of the four, arguing shares already fully embed low double-digit room night growth and margin expansion through 2028. The stock's performance supports that reading: a company beating and raising guidance across every metric has still lost roughly a fifth of its value in a month.
Some caution traces to capital allocation.
On September 14, Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) announced a $250 million Housing Accelerator program, starting with a roughly 200-unit development in Austin. Chesky framed it as getting ahead of housing affordability criticism, and management said returns will run below market rates, doing little for near-term profitability and potentially inviting more regulatory scrutiny.
Hedge funds holding long Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) positions fell to 75 from 87 in Q2, though some added meaningfully: AQR Capital increased its stake 33% to 10,624,015 shares worth $1.52 billion, and Holocene Advisors grew its position 147% to 1,951,914 shares worth $279.3 million. Harris Associates, the largest holder, trimmed 2% to 18,861,551 shares worth $2.7 billion.
Short interest rose to 14.23 million shares as of August 31 from 12.91 million a month earlier.
Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) trades at 25.38x forward earnings as of September 24, nearly double Booking Holdings' 13.28x, leaving little cushion if Hotels or AI monetization disappoint.
Four analysts raised targets this month on accelerating core growth, a fast-growing Hotels segment, and visible AI cost savings, yet the stock moved directly against that consensus.
Morgan Stanley's more guarded call, the only one not to raise its target into the $200s, indicates growth and margin expansion are already priced in.
Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) likely needs Hotels to keep scaling and the housing initiative to stay a background story before the stock can catch up with the upgrades.

Introduction: One year after saying Airbnb would become an "AI-first application," the company declared it had "rebuilt itself as an AI-native company."
On August 6, 2025, Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky stated during an earnings call,
In the coming years, Airbnb will become an "AI-first application."

One year later, on August 6, 2026, Airbnb declared in its earnings announcement that it had fundamentally rebuilt Airbnb as an "AI-native company."
The conversation has shifted from the app to the nature of the company itself.
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
"So, what is the AI-first organization that Airbnb is aiming for?"
The headline "AI wrote 60% of the code" does not answer this question.
While the 60% figure indicates a change in the volume of work, it does not explain who is doing what within the organization.
I interpret the basis for the AI-first organization Airbnb is aiming for by dividing it into two categories.
The first is the materials Airbnb has released to investors, such as earnings announcements, earnings calls, and filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
The second is the content shared by Ahmad Al-Dahle, who became CTO in January 2026, in an interview with AI-specialized media outlet Latent Space (published October 2, 2026).
Airbnb CTO Al-Dahle previously served as the head of generative AI at Meta and led the development of "Llama," the AI model that Meta released for anyone to use.
"Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience"
The earnings materials show the results achieved in numbers, while the CTO's interview describes the target organizational image in words.
Notably, Latent Space has named Airbnb's approach "inside-out AI." This term is used by Latent Space and is not Airbnb's own terminology.
Inside-Out AI: Rebuilding Airbnb Behind the Scenes and Across the Guest Experience

Figure 1: Airbnb's earnings show the destination in numbers, while the CTO describes the target organizational image in words
Chapter 1: Airbnb handed over coding tasks and primary customer support to AI
First, I will list the milestones that can be confirmed in the earnings materials.
As of the first quarter of 2026, approximately 60% of the code generated by engineers at Airbnb is written in collaboration with AI.
CEO Chesky described this same figure as "written by AI" during the earnings call, adding that Airbnb estimates this to be roughly double the industry average.
The scope of this figure is "code generated by engineers," not the entirety of Airbnb's existing codebase.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
The number of features and improvements released between January and June 2026 increased by approximately 80% compared to the same six-month period the previous year. For major initiatives, the time from conception to delivery was reduced by up to 60%.
For customer support, an AI assistant serves as the first point of contact for inquiries.
The percentage of consultations initiated by the AI assistant that were resolved without human intervention rose from approximately one-third in the October-December 2025 quarter to over 40% in the January-March 2026 quarter. By the April-June quarter, this reached approximately 45%, and the number of supported languages exceeded 50.
The denominator is "consultations initiated by the AI assistant," not all inquiries.
As of August 2025, this AI assistant was built by combining 13 models and fine-tuning them with tens of thousands of conversations.
Figure 2: Airbnb support features an AI assistant that responds first, while maintaining a path to human agents.
The change is also reflected in costs.
Support costs per booking in the April-June quarter fell by approximately 16% year-over-year. During the earnings call, CEO Chesky explained the reason, stating, "Part of it is due to improvements in the AI assistant."
Airbnb reports Q2 2026 financial results.
In the August 2026 earnings call, CFO Ellie Mertz stated that "the vast majority is due to AI agents."
The AI agents referred to here are the support AI assistants.
There is some variation in how management describes the reasons for the same figures.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The quarterly report (10-Q) filed with the SEC is a bit more specific.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, the use of AI in support reduced the number of inquiries handled by human agents, resulting in a $17 million reduction in costs paid to external contractors.
At Airbnb, much of the coding work and the initial response to inquiries have been handed over to AI.
What remains for engineers after coding work shifts to AI is covered in another article, so please refer to it below👇
Chapter 2: Airbnb changed its approach to giving small teams clear missions and releasing features as soon as they are ready.
CEO Chesky has repeatedly explained the methodology behind these numbers during earnings calls.
Give small, elite teams clear missions, release simple improvements to learn, and focus efforts on what works.
In the February 2026 earnings call, Chesky stated that he began this approach two years ago and expanded it company-wide after confirming it worked.
They have also stopped hoarding features for launch events, releasing them as soon as they are ready.
Regarding the performance for the April-June 2026 quarter, CEO Chesky stated that the reason was not a single product or initiative, but a combination of execution, talent, and an AI-accelerated approach.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
Airbnb, Inc. "Q2 2026 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
CEO Chesky does not view the utilization rate of AI tools as a metric for success.
He called the figure that over 80% of engineers use AI tools a "vanity metric," stating that what matters is the company's culture and its ability to adapt to change.
Airbnb, Inc. "Q4 2025 Earnings Call" Corrected Transcript
The role of humans is also beginning to change.
CEO Chesky stated that Airbnb "must move at the speed of AI," indicating that management roles focused solely on overseeing people will not be as necessary as they once were. He also mentioned that design and engineering managers are returning to hands-on coding work.
Investing.com "Earnings call transcript: Airbnb Q1 2026 misses EPS but beats revenue"
CTO Al-Dahle goes even further.
He ended the practice of creating requirements documents and handing them off from designers to engineers, instead having planning, design, and development teams deliberate from the start using working prototypes.
Al-Dahle's belief is that companies organized by purpose and outcome, rather than by function, are stronger in the AI era.
However, regarding the future of team structure, Chesky himself stated that "it is too early to say." Organization by outcome is the CTO's policy and is not the final form of the company known as Airbnb.
What about the number of people? At the end of 2025, there were approximately 8,200 employees.
In the April-June 2026 quarter, personnel expenses in the operations and support departments increased by $27 million due to an increase in average headcount. The number of employees has not decreased.
Marts explains that because the output and speed obtained from current employees have increased significantly, there is no need to increase headcount as much as in the past.
Chapter 3: Airbnb has kept the judgment of complex and sensitive cases in the hands of employees
While there are tasks that Airbnb has handed over to AI, there are also judgments that have been left in human hands.
According to the annual report (10-K) filed with the SEC, as of the end of 2025, Airbnb has entrusted the majority of support inquiries to approximately 13,000 outsourced personnel. Internal support employees focus on complex and sensitive cases.
CEO Chesky called AI-based customer support the "hardest problem for AI." This is because incorrect answers are not permitted, and urgent cases or matters involving trust and safety must be accurately handed over to humans.
CTO Al-Dahle also says that they intentionally choose which cases to have AI solve and decide which cases not to leave to AI yet.
Even in the development field, a line is drawn between AI and humans.
According to CTO Al-Dahle, many teams have begun automating system monitoring and primary response to failures (on-call).
When a monitoring alert is triggered, an agent (a mechanism where AI proceeds with procedures on its own) is activated to determine whether it is a problem. If there is a problem, it issues a pull request (a proposal for code changes; hereafter PR), and an engineer reviews the PR.
If it is a false alarm, the agent closes the case itself.
Figure 3: A diagram of the flow where an agent determines Airbnb's on-call status and a human reviews the PR
The name of the figure above is "Handed over to agents," but CTO Al-Dahle's words are that many teams are "beginning" automation.
In the on-call flow, the initial determination of whether it is a problem is handled by an agent. What remains for humans is the judgment of whether or not to incorporate the PR proposed by the agent as code.
Figure 4: Airbnb separates where AI is entrusted with primary judgment and where humans make judgments
CEO Chesky also stated that regarding AI spending, he judges not by the amount of tokens (units of text processed by AI) used, but by how much product was released and the quality of the design.
It is also humans who decide not to make AI usage volume itself a goal.
Chapter 4: CTO Al-Dahle requires that even for PRs written by AI, the person who created them must explain them
What Airbnb leaves as a human role is not just judgment.
What CTO Al-Dahle strongly demands is that every engineer be able to explain what they created, even if it is a PR created by AI.

Behind the above is a concern for young engineers.
Experienced engineers have acquired judgment through the experience of shipping systems, running them in production, and failing.
Now that AI handles many tasks, can young people gain the same experience?

Booking (BKNG) vs Airbnb (ABNB): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
Booking Earns More on Every Dollar:
The operating gap between them is wider than their reputations suggest. Booking turns 34.41% of revenue into operating profit. Airbnb manages 21.01%.
That thirteen-point gap is the whole difference between the two models. Booking lists rooms somebody else built, insured, and staffed, while Airbnb has to police millions of individual hosts it does not employ.
The cash follows. Booking produced $7.73 billion of levered free cash flow against $3.21 billion at Airbnb. Earnings grew 117.90% at Booking in the most recent quarter, which is not the profile of a business in decline.

Airbnb Grows Faster and Owes Nothing:
Here is what the share prices have been responding to. Airbnb grew revenue 16.50% in the most recent quarter against 8.10% at Booking. For investors paying for growth rather than for margin, that is the number that matters.
The balance sheets are a genuine contrast. Airbnb holds $12.07 billion of cash against $2.50 billion of debt, so its enterprise value of $78.62 billion sits well below its market value of $88.19 billion. Booking is the other way round, with $20.92 billion of debt against $17.21 billion of cash.
Airbnb also earns 34.54% on equity, which is a strong figure and reflects how little capital the business needs. The supply is the difference nobody can copy quickly. Airbnb's inventory is millions of homes that no hotel chain owns, and no competitor can simply build.
Booking is the cheaper of the two and one of the few large travel names trading below the market multiple. You can find more of them here.
The Valuation Case:
Sustainability sits with Booking. Hotel commissions recur because hotels have no better way to fill empty rooms, and the business has survived every attempt to disintermediate it.
Airbnb's growth is faster, but its supply is individual hosts, who are more easily tempted elsewhere than a hotel chain with a distribution contract.
On price, the gap is stark. Booking trades at 13.28 times forward estimates against 25.38 times for Airbnb, so an investor pays roughly half as much for each dollar of next year's profit.
The PEG ratio settles whether that discount is deserved. Booking's is 0.61 and Airbnb's is 1.42, which means the cheaper stock is cheap even after adjusting for its slower growth. We ranked the alternatives here.
Conclusion:
Booking is the better of the two. It earns a wider margin, produces more than twice the free cash flow, trades at little more than half the forward multiple, and has fallen a quarter while its earnings more than doubled last quarter. However, Airbnb is growing twice as fast and carries net cash rather than net debt. It also owns supply that cannot be recreated. An investor choosing Booking is being paid to accept slower growth, which on these multiples looks like the better trade.

Operational Differentiation and Network Insulation
Airbnb, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:ABNB) operational model relies on a highly fragmented, non-standardized supply base that inherently resists simple aggregation. Unlike traditional online travel agencies that distribute uniform hotel rooms through centralized global distribution systems, the company offers over 9 million active listings managed directly by private hosts. Standardizing or crawling millions of independent property listings, house rules, pricing algorithms, and individual host communications presents a significant hurdle for autonomous AI booking agents.
In addition, the company's direct traffic profile remains among the strongest in the digital consumer space, with nearly 90% of traffic coming direct or organically. The direct consumer relationship insulates the business from rising search engine marketing costs while posting a 35% adjusted EBITDA margin in the second quarter
Valuation, Relative Premium, and Downside Risks
Trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of roughly 25.4x, Airbnb, Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) carries a significant valuation premium over the broader sector median of 14.55x. While the premium highlights the company's superior cash conversion, strong net cash position, and dominant brand mindshare, it also creates a valuation risk if travel demand decelerates. High valuation multiples leave little margin for error if macroeconomic pressures dampen international leisure spending or if regulatory tightening across major metropolitan markets limits inventory growth. If booking growth slows, the stock's elevated multiple could face compression regardless of its competitive insulation against AI competitors.

delivered some of our strongest results in years. In Q2, that momentum accelerated as we exceeded our outlook across every key metric. Revenue grew 17% year-over-year to $3.6 billion. GBV grew 16% year-over-year to $27.2 billion, driven by continued

billion, representing an expansion in Adjusted EBITDA Margin to 35%. One of the most encouraging trends in Q2 was that we saw year-over-year growth accelerate not just in our expansion markets, but in many of our largest core markets as well. In
fact, net origin nights booked in the U.S., France, the UK, and Australia all accelerated in Q2, reinforcing our confidence that our product innovation is driving demand across our business. We’ve rebuilt Airbnb from the ground up to be an
AI-native company, and it’s showing up in our results. AI, combined with an exceptional team and better execution, is why we’re building and iterating faster than ever before. On key initiatives, we’ve reduced the time from concept
to delivery by as much as 60%. And compared to the same period last year, we’ve increased the number of features and improvements we’ve shipped this year by nearly 80%. This faster pace of innovation is reshaping nearly every part of
Airbnb and we believe it’s one of the reasons we’re outperforming our largest peers. Here are some highlights from the quarter: Making Airbnb better for guests and hosts Over the past two quarters, we’ve talked about our blueprint
for improving Airbnb through hundreds of small improvements that compound over time. Those improvements are making it easier to book, easier to host, and driving growth across the business. For guests Search and discovery - With millions of homes
and a growing selection of services and experiences on Airbnb, we improved search and discovery to help guests quickly find the right options for every trip. ¦ A redesigned homepage: Guests now see more relevant recommendations for listings,
experiences, services, and destinations. ¦ Smarter search rankings: Search results prioritize higher-quality homes that are a better fit for each trip. ¦ Detailed neighborhood maps: Guests can explore nearby restaurants, landmarks, and
transportation to better understand the neighborhoods where they’re staying. Login and sign-up - Every additional step before booking can create friction. We redesigned login and sign-up to help more guests access Airbnb and start booking.
¦ Redesigned sign-up and login: Guests can now create an account and sign in more easily across iOS, Android, and web. ¦ Added flexibility: Guests have additional ways to access their account, helping reduce login failures and customer

rence between browsing and booking. We expanded payment options and streamlined checkout to reduce friction and help more guests complete their booking. ¦ Reserve Now, Pay Later: Guests can now use Reserve Now, Pay Later on more listings in
more countries, and they’ll see it more often throughout the booking journey. ¦ Flexible cancellation policies: Guests can more easily understand their cancellation options before booking. ¦ Updated checkout: Checkout now surfaces
the most relevant promotions and credits for each guest, as well as eligible payment options. ¦ Interest-free installments: Eligible guests in Mexico and Brazil can now pay with interest- free installments. For hosts Pricing - Effective pricing
is one of the biggest drivers of host success. We introduced simpler pricing and more flexible cancellation policies to help hosts succeed. ¦ Simplified pricing in Airbnb Setup: New hosts can more easily set die ff rent weekday and weekend
rates. ¦ Single service fee for API hosts: Hosts can more easily set the same price guests see. ¦ Updated cancellation policies: We migrated eligible listings from Strict to Firm cancellation policies, helping hosts attract more bookings.

luggage storage. These services address some of the biggest pain points guests face while traveling. And we recently introduced resort passes, giving guests day access to amenities at some of the world’s best hotels. It’s still early
days, but we’re seeing real momentum—both in guests’ bookings and how quickly we’re scaling these partner services. ¦ Airbnb Experiences: We added thousands of new Experiences across our most in-demand categories,
increasing Airbnb Experiences supply by nearly 80% year-over-year in Q2 2026. As our selection grew, demand grew alongside it, with seats booked accelerating year-over- year and quarter-over-quarter. ¦ Boutique and independent hotels: We added

more people to become hosts, and help cities welcome more visitors. The brand awareness and trust these partnerships create can benefit our business long after the event ends. The FIFA World Cup 2026™ is one recent example of this strategy in

economic uplift for the local community. Beyond the World Cup, we’re building a repeatable playbook that scales across global, regional, and local events. Partners include the International Olympic Committee, Tour de France, Art Basel fairs,
Lollapalooza festivals, La Liga in Spain, and most recently NASCAR. As we expand these partnerships, we’ll continue strengthening the Airbnb brand and supporting travel demand in destinations around the world. 6
